title: Becoming a Cultural Being: A Dynamic Systems View of Human Development
abstract: This paper proposes a dynamical systems account of human cultural development grounded in a process-relational worldview. In contrast to mechanistic approaches that treat culture as an external influence on development, this framework conceptualizes culture and development as inseparable, co-constituting processes that unfold across situational, ontogenetic, and sociocultural levels. Drawing on infant–caregiver interactions as a “slices of life” example, we illustrate how culturally patterned routines emerge, stabilize and transform through self-organization, and how historical, material and sociocultural conditions afford and constrain developmental trajectories. We apply key concepts from the dynamic systems approach, including emergence, self-organization, attractor stabilization, circular causality, and historical constraint, to explain human cultural development. We treat emergent processual structures as formal causes and adopt explanatory pluralism. Inspired by the work of Vygotsky, Rogoff, and dynamic systems theorists, we propose a prototheoretical framework for reconceptualising, systematising, and advancing integrative, process-oriented explanations of human cultural development.
